lesson.title: The Preoperational Stage: Big Imagination, Not-Yet-Logical Thinking
lesson.summary: Between roughly ages two and seven, children develop language and symbolic, imaginative thought at a remarkable pace, but Piaget showed that their reasoning is still governed more by how things look than by logic.
lesson.body:
The mental representation that began emerging near the end of the sensorimotor stage becomes the dominant mode of thought in the preoperational stage, which Piaget placed at roughly age two to seven. Children in this stage undergo an explosion of language ability and become able to use symbols, meaning that words, images, and pretend objects can stand in for real things. A child pushing a block across the floor while making engine noises is using exactly this kind of symbolic thought, and the elaborate pretend play so common at this age is one of its most visible signs.

Piaget's name for this stage, "preoperational," points to what is still missing rather than what has been gained: children this age do not yet reliably perform mental operations, meaning logical actions that can be reversed. Several specific limitations follow from this. Egocentrism describes difficulty seeing a situation from another person's point of view. Piaget and his colleague Barbel Inhelder illustrated this with their well known three mountains task, in which young children, shown a model of three mountains, struggled to identify what the scene would look like from a different vantage point and instead described their own view. Centration describes the tendency to focus on just one striking feature of a situation while ignoring others. Irreversibility describes difficulty mentally reversing a sequence of steps to work backward. And animism describes the tendency to attribute life, feelings, or intentions to objects that are not actually alive, such as insisting that the sun follows you or that a toy is sad.

These limitations show up most clearly, and most famously, in conservation tasks, which get their own chapter next. In brief, conservation is the understanding that a quantity stays the same even when its appearance changes, and preoperational children generally fail at this, insisting, for example, that a tall thin glass holds more liquid than a short wide one even after watching the same amount of liquid poured between them.

It is worth holding both halves of this picture together. Preoperational children are making enormous cognitive gains, especially in language and imaginative, symbolic play, even while their logical reasoning is still tied to how things appear rather than how they actually work. That combination of expanding imagination and still-developing logic is the defining character of this stage.
